via RNZ Pacific News

House Agriculture Committee visits Samoa on fact-finding trip of poultry industry

2026-11-18

Sees the success of the strong partnership between private sector and govt

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — A group of American Samoa lawmakers returned recently after a weeklong visit to Samoa with a clear message: while the poultry industry in the neighboring island nation is rapidly expanding and investing in large-scale production, the territory remains heavily dependent on imported eggs and poultry products to meet local demand.

That was the consensus shared by members of the House Agriculture Committee following their seven-day fact-finding trip to Samoa. The delegation was led by Committee Chairman Tiaoalii Fauagiga Sai and included Vice Chairman Ape Mike Asifoa and committee member Representative Luaitaua Gene Pan. They were accompanied by Samoa Consul General in American Samoa, Fata Brian Kaio, and House Counsel Seiuli Alvin Tuala.

According to the lawmakers, the visit provided a firsthand look at the significant growth taking place in Samoa's agricultural sector, particularly in poultry production. The delegation toured farming operations, met with industry representatives, and discussed opportunities for greater collaboration between the two Samoas.

They noted that Samoa has made substantial investments in modern poultry facilities and is steadily increasing its capacity to supply locally produced eggs and chicken products, reducing its dependence on imports while creating new economic opportunities for local farmers and businesses.

The lawmakers said the trip highlighted the contrast between Samoa's expanding poultry industry and American Samoa's continued reliance on imported poultry products, raising important questions about food security, agricultural development, and the potential for strengthening local production in the territory.

Led by major agri-business operators such as the Frankie and Ah Liki groups, Samoa's poultry industry has experienced significant growth in recent years. With strong backing from the Samoa Government and its agricultural development programs, producers have invested heavily in modern poultry facilities, expanded egg production, and increased local chicken meat processing in an effort to reduce the country's reliance on imported poultry products.

Lawmakers who visited Samoa said the industry's rapid expansion reflects a coordinated strategy between the government and private sector to strengthen food security, create jobs, and keep more food production within the country. They noted that large-scale poultry farms are now producing substantial quantities of eggs and chicken products, helping Samoa move closer to meeting local demand through domestic production rather than imports.

Sunshine Pacific Farm, a subsidiary of Frankie's Company Ltd., is one of Samoa's largest commercial poultry operations. The company built poultry houses in Tanumalala for egg production in 2019 with a capacity of about 19,500 birds, added more poultry houses in 2021, and now has the capacity to produce up to 3,000 dozen eggs per day.

The success of Samoa's growing poultry industry was also highlighted by Taimalie Charlie Westerlund, owner of Tanumapua Poultry Farm, which is part of the Ah Liki Investment Group. Speaking with members of the delegation, Westerlund proudly pointed to the farm's achievements, noting that its locally produced eggs now account for approximately 75 percent of egg sales in Samoa's retail market.

Westerlund said consumer demand for locally produced eggs continues to grow because of their freshness and quality, giving them a competitive edge over imported products.

"Our eggs are of higher quality, healthier, and certainly much fresher than imported eggs," Westerlund said. "Consumers can tell the difference. At the same time, we're offering them at very reasonable prices, which makes locally produced eggs an attractive option for families and businesses alike."

The American Samoa delegation, who tasted the eggs every morning during their one-week visit, agreed wholeheartedly.

"They were delicious," said an impressed Representative Ape Mike Asifoa said. "The Samoa poultry industry is a success story that American Samoa would do well to emulate."

According to Asifoa, the delegation was informed that Samoa's rapidly growing poultry sector has reached a stage where locally produced eggs now supply the vast majority of the domestic market, dramatically reducing the country's dependence on imported eggs. He said industry leaders are confident that, with continued investment and government support, Samoa is on track to achieve full self-sufficiency in egg production in the near future.

"The level of growth we witnessed was remarkable," Asifoa said. "What stood out most was the strong partnership between the government and private sector. Their efforts are producing real results, and the country is now far less reliant on imported eggs than it was just a few years ago. They are very close to being able to meet all local demand with eggs produced right there in Samoa."

In contrast, he pointed out that there is very little large-scale commercial poultry production in American Samoa. Most chicken meat and eggs are imported, although there are some small local producers and backyard operations. The sole official egg production operation, the Taputimu Farm Fresh Eggs located in Taputimu village, is owned by Bill and Nancy Satele and has been operating since 1976.

Despite the presence of a long-established local egg farm, American Samoa has been unable to produce enough eggs to satisfy territory-wide demand. Industry observers point to high feed costs, shipping expenses, limited economies of scale, labor shortages, and other operational challenges as major obstacles to expanding local production, leaving the territory heavily dependent on imported eggs.

The local chicken meat farm and processing plant at Mulifanua is also growing rapidly, and lawmakers were told that if the sector continues its current trajectory, it could create new economic opportunities for villages, church groups, community organizations, and individual families interested in poultry farming.

Industry representatives explained that the two major companies driving the sector have developed a partnership model designed to benefit both the businesses and local communities. Under the arrangement, interested groups and individuals can purchase young chickens from the companies and raise them on their own farms using feeding programs and animal-care practices recommended by company technicians.

This is important as the chickens used in the operation are specially bred meat-producing birds, commonly known as broilers, which are imported from overseas. These birds are specifically developed for rapid growth, efficient feed conversion, and high meat yield, allowing them to reach market weight in a relatively short period of time. Unlike traditional village chickens raised primarily for eggs or household consumption, broilers are bred exclusively for commercial meat production.

Broilers are imported when they are one day old and are fed and nurtured until they are strong enough to be sold to interested community members. Once they reach market size, the farmers can then sell them back to the company for processing, packaging, and distribution. The system provides a guaranteed market for growers while enabling the companies to increase production without having to raise all of the birds themselves.

According to those involved in the industry, the approach has the potential to generate new sources of income for families and village communities while helping Samoa expand local chicken meat production and reduce its reliance on imported poultry products. Members of Parliament were told that the model is also benefiting constituencies by creating economic activity at the grassroots level and allowing more people to participate directly in the country's growing poultry industry.

Representative Asifoa described the delegation's visit to Sunshine Pacific's chicken meat farm and processing plant at Mulifanua as an eye-opening experience that underscored the importance of a strong partnership between government and the private sector.

He said the operation demonstrated how coordinated investments in agriculture cannot only stimulate economic growth but also strengthen a country's food security and resilience in the face of unforeseen disruptions.

According to Asifoa, discussions with Samoa's Minister for Agriculture and Fisheries, Fuimaono Maiava Tito Asafo, and Ministry Chief Executive Officer Afamasaga Taimalietane Matatumua focused on fostering closer cooperation between the two Samoas and exploring pathways to facilitate the export of fresh Samoan eggs and poultry products to American Samoa.

However, Asifoa noted that the primary challenge remains compliance with the requirements of the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS), which regulates the importation of animal products into the United States and its territories to prevent the introduction and spread of poultry diseases.

He said ministry officials informed the delegation that Samoa has not yet submitted a formal application seeking approval to export its poultry products to American Samoa. Despite this, Asifoa stressed that the visit highlighted valuable lessons for the territory and reinforced the need for American Samoa's Department of Agriculture to take a more proactive role in developing the local poultry industry.

"We cannot continue relying almost entirely on imported food products," Asifoa said. "What we saw in Samoa shows what can be achieved when government and private businesses work together toward a common goal. Developing our own poultry industry will not only improve food security but could also create new economic opportunities for families, community groups, and entrepreneurs throughout the territory."

He emphasized that expanding local egg and poultry production should be viewed as a long-term investment in American Samoa's food security and self-sufficiency.

Asifoa noted that recent global and transportation-related events highlight the vulnerability of island communities that rely heavily on imported goods.

He pointed to the recent Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) order grounding departing flights across the United States due to safety concerns, as well as the ongoing conflict involving Iran, as examples of situations that can disrupt international transportation networks. Such events, he said, can have a ripple effect on American Samoa by affecting shipping schedules, delaying cargo deliveries, and potentially reducing the availability of essential imported goods on local store shelves.

"The government needs to be prepared," he emphasized. "It doesn't hurt to be prepared, but it will certainly hurt if we are not prepared." He said the territory cannot afford to wait until a supply-chain crisis occurs before taking steps to strengthen local food production and reduce its dependence on imported goods.

Am Samoa Bar Association holds first High School Mock Trial Competition

2026-11-16

Students try a fictional murder case as ASBA sets its sights on the 2028 Nationals

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The American Samoa Bar Association (ASBA) congratulates the students, coaches and schools who took part in the inaugural American Samoa High School Mock Trial Competition, which concluded on November 12 with a championship round at the High Court of American Samoa.

Tafuna High School and Samoana High School met in the final, with Samoana High School named the champion.

Eight teams from seven schools competed: Faga'itua High School (FHS), Leone High School (LHS), Manumalo Baptist High School (MBHS), Nu'uuli Vocational Technical High School (NVTHS), two teams from Pacific Horizon High School (PHHS), Samoana High School (SHS) and Tafuna High School (THS).

Students stepped into the roles of attorneys, witnesses, clerks and bailiffs to try a fictional criminal case — American Samoa Government v. Olena Molia. In the case, restaurant owner Olena Molia is charged with first-degree murder in the death of her business partner, Toni Lua, at their restaurant in Tafuna.

The prosecution argues that Molia acted after discovering that Lua had been stealing from the business, and that she stood to gain half a million dollars from her partner's death. The defense contends that someone else is responsible, pointing to a loan shark to whom Lua owed more than two hundred thousand dollars.

The case featured six witnesses and twelve exhibits, and teams had to be ready to argue either side.

The preliminary rounds were held on November 2 at the Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) Courthouse, where NVTHS, MBHS, SHS, and THS advanced.

In the semifinals on November 3, also at the ALJ Courthouse, THS defeated MBHS and SHS defeated NVTHS. The championship round followed on Nov. 12th at the High Court.

Students were scored on their preparation, communication and courtroom performance rather than on the legal merits of the case.

Attorney General Gwen Tauiliili-Langkilde and La'apui Ale judged the first day of competition. Administrative Law Judge Roy Hall presided over the semifinals, and Associate Justice Sunia and Acting Associate Justice Patea judged the championship final.

“Mock trial gives our students something a classroom cannot: the experience of standing in a real courtroom, thinking on their feet, and making their case with respect for the other side,” said ASBA President Lornalei Meredith. “The young people we saw this month showed the confidence and character our community needs, whether or not they choose a career in law.”

The ASBA extends its sincere thanks to the judges for giving their time and expertise, and to the volunteer attorneys, coaches, teachers, court staff and families who made the competition possible. The ASBA also thanks the Department of Education’s Secondary Division, School Lunch Program, Educational Technical Division for their partnership and support.

Building on this first competition, the ASBA is working toward entering a team to represent American Samoa at the 2028 National High School Mock Trial Championship.

The American Samoa Bar Association is the official bar association and licensing body for attorneys practicing law in American Samoa. The ASBA works to promote justice, the rule of law and a strong legal system through public education, legislative review, support for the judiciary and advocacy for the rule of law.

Through programs like the High School Mock Trial Competition, the ASBA works to build understanding of the justice system and encourage the next generation of leaders in the territory.

(Contact: Bernadine Ott | bernadine@meredithsunia.com)

Thanksgiving Food Safety: Do's and Don'ts

2026-11-13

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Thanksgiving is a time to gather, share a meal, and celebrate. Follow these food safety tips from the Nebraska Poison Center to help prevent food borne illness.

DO: Follow These Food Safety Tips

    •    Wash your hands. Use soap and warm water for at least 20 seconds before and after handling food.

    •    Thaw turkey safely. Thaw in the refrigerator (allow 24 hours for every 4 to 5 pounds; A 24-pound turkey may take 5 to 6 days to thaw in the refrigerator) or in cold water (allow 30 minutes per pound, changing the water every 30 minutes). Never thaw at room temperature. Cook cold-water-thawed turkey immediately.

    •    Cook turkey thoroughly. Use a food thermometer to ensure the thickest part of the breast and innermost parts of the thigh and wing reach 165°F.

    •    Cook stuffing separately. For the safest option, prepare stuffing in a separate baking dish. If you do stuff the turkey, do so loosely and immediately before cooking and verify the center reaches 165°F.

    •    Refrigerate leftovers promptly. Refrigerate turkey, stuffing, and gravy within 2 hours. Store in separate, shallow containers.

    •    Use leftovers within these time limits:

    •    Turkey and stuffing: 3 to 4 days.

    •    Gravy: 1 to 2 days.

DON'T: Take These Food Safety Risks

    •    Don't leave perishable foods at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

    •    Don't set your oven temperature below 325°F.

    •    Don't prepare food when you are sick.

    •    Don't rely on appearance to determine whether turkey is fully cooked. Always use a food thermometer.

    •    Don't stuff your turkey unless you can verify the center of the stuffing reaches 165°F.

Need help preparing your turkey?

Visit Butterball's website or call the Butterball Turkey Talk-Line at 1-800-288-8372.

Need Help? Contact the Nebraska Poison Center.

Call 1-800-222-1222 to speak with a registered nurse, advanced practice registered nurse or pharmacist, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year.

Disagreements surface over renovation of historic building housing the Territorial Registrar’s Office

2026-11-13

By

Asi Andrew Fa'asau

andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — One of the few remaining landmark structures from the U.S. Naval Administration era in American Samoa is currently undergoing renovation as efforts continue to preserve an important piece of the territory's history. The project also includes plans to construct a fence around the building to tackle a longstanding litter problem beneath its surrounding awning.

And, while the PNRS Board approved the proposed improvements, the debate has highlighted the enduring importance of preserving one of American Samoa's last remaining links to the U.S. Naval Administration era and ensuring that any changes made today respect its historical significance for generations to come.

THE RENOVATION PROJECT

Located in the heart of downtown Fagatogo, it was originally constructed in 1917 during the Naval Administration period as a U.S. Navy radio communications station. The facility played a vital role in maintaining communications between American Samoa and other U.S. military and government outposts across the Pacific.

The historic building is now home to the Office of the Territorial Registrar, a division of the Department of Legal Affairs under the Attorney General's Office.

Last week, Attorney General Gwen Tauiliili-Langkilde appeared before a public hearing of the Project Notification and Review System (PNRS) Board to seek approval for additional improvements to be incorporated into an existing land-use permit for the project.

The Attorney General told board members that the project is being carried out in two phases. She explained that Phase One, which is already underway, focuses on renovating and restoring the interior of the historic building. Phase Two would involve improvements to the exterior, including the installation of a new roof, the addition of a gutter system, and the construction of a perimeter fence.

According to Tauiliili-Langkilde, the exterior upgrades are intended to complement the ongoing interior restoration while helping to preserve the building's long-term structural integrity. She noted that the improvements would provide greater protection from the elements, help prevent rainwater damage, and reduce future maintenance needs.

With regard to the re-roofing component of the project, the Attorney General told board members that the existing roof is deteriorating and requires upgrading with stronger, more durable roofing materials capable of withstanding the Territory's harsh weather conditions.

She noted that there are currently open spaces beneath the eaves that allow rain, wind, and pests, including rats and other rodents, to enter the structure. Closing these gaps, she said, would help protect the building from deterioration while improving its overall security and preservation.

Tauiliili-Langkilde also explained that the installation of a gutter system is an important component of the proposed exterior improvements because the building currently has no gutters to collect and channel rainwater. As a result, water runoff flows directly from the roof onto the surrounding area, increasing the risk of water damage over time. The proposed gutter system would redirect rainwater into the existing drainage network, helping to protect both the building and its foundation.

In explaining the proposed fence, she noted it would enhance security and assist in addressing the persistent littering problem around the property.

The sheltered area beneath the building's surrounding awning has become a popular gathering spot for travelers arriving and departing on inter-island ferries to Manu'a and Apia, as well as those waiting to be picked up by family members or transportation providers. Officials say the persistent accumulation of trash in the area prompted the Governor's Office to include the fence as part of the building's improvement and preservation efforts.

Tauiliili-Langkilde further emphasized that the property is situated in one of the busiest and most heavily congested areas of Fagatogo.

The building faces the main roadway into the downtown area and is flanked by the access road leading to the inter-island ferry wharf. In addition, a secondary access road runs behind the structure and is frequently used by vehicles delivering or collecting cargo, packages, and pallets of goods.

Tauiliili-Langkilde told board members that the proposed fence would help establish a clear boundary around the historic property, improve security, and protect the building from damage caused by the high volume of vehicle and pedestrian traffic. She added that the fence would also help preserve the site's appearance and integrity while complementing the broader restoration effort aimed at safeguarding one of the Territory's historic landmarks.

PUBLIC CONCERNS

Plans to install a perimeter fence around the building drew the strongest criticism from several members of the public, who argued that such a feature would detract from the historic character and visual appeal of the landmark. Opponents contended that enclosing the structure with a fence would make it resemble a mausoleum or secured compound, diminishing its prominence and aesthetic value in the heart of the town.

One staunch critic, Jim McGuire, a longtime resident who is currently a member of the Zoning Board, described the justification for the proposed fence as superficial and unconvincing. According to McGuire, concerns about travelers using the area beneath the building's awning as a waiting area could be addressed through simpler and more practical measures that would not compromise the building's appearance.

"The government is looking at spending a substantial amount of money on a fence that may not even solve the underlying issue," he said. "A far more practical and cost-effective solution would be for the Registrar's Office to hire a casual worker whose responsibility would be to keep the grounds and surrounding area clean and well maintained. The office could also install signs reminding people not to litter and provide adequate trash bins for public use. It's really that simple.

"Instead of spending taxpayer dollars on a fence that could detract from the appearance of one of American Samoa's historic landmarks, the government should focus on basic maintenance and public awareness. Keeping the area clean, providing proper waste disposal facilities, and ensuring regular upkeep would address the problem without compromising the beauty and historical character of the building."

McGuire, who attended the PNRS public hearing as a member of the public, argued that the historic building should remain as open and visible to the public as possible. He said that, as one of the few surviving structures from the U.S. Naval Administration era, it should not be surrounded by barriers that could diminish public access to and appreciation of an important part of American Samoa's history.

When PNRS Board Chairman Tino Ma'o gave members of the public and the media the opportunity to ask questions about the proposed project, McGuire asked the attorney general whether the proposal should be referred first to the Zoning Board for consideration, arguing that the PNRS Board's primary focus is environmental and land-use matters.

He also noted that the board's eight members are government representatives and questioned whether there had been sufficient public input on a proposal affecting one of the Territory's most significant historic landmarks.

"As I mentioned, that building has been there since 1917," the AG responded. "It was there first. If anything, anything new around it needs to go to the Zoning Board. That building was the first on the block, so to speak."

McGuire also argued that the Office of the Territorial Registrar should be relocated to a safer location on higher ground, away from areas vulnerable to flooding during heavy rainfall or natural disasters such as tsunamis. He pointed out that the building was flooded during the last tsunami, damaging priceless legal documents kept there. He said it has never been disclosed how much it cost the government to send the water-damaged files off-island to be dry-frozen in an attempt to save the ink.

"The Office of the Territorial Registrar is entrusted with preserving some of the Territory's most important historical and legal records, so it should be housed in a facility that offers greater protection from natural hazards," he said. "A more suitable location would be the Lumana'i Building directly across the street."

Responding to this suggestion, AG Tauiliili-Langkilde pointed out that the Lumana'i Building is "privately, semi-autonomously owned" by the American Samoa Development Bank.

"So if we move the Territorial Registrar's Office to the Lumana'i Building, people like you who have used that building since 1975 and me, who have used it since 1993, will have to pay more fees for the use of that building because it's not going to be free," the attorney general explained.

In an interview with McGuire after the hearing, he admitted that he forgot to point out to AG Tauiliili-Langkilde that the Lumana'i Building is owned by a government entity, so it should be possible to negotiate a reduced rental rate in recognition of the vital public service provided by the Registrar's Office.

"Unlike other government agencies, it is not a major revenue-generating office, yet it is responsible for safeguarding records that are of immense historical, legal, and cultural importance to the Territory," McGuire argued. "Those records deserve to be protected in a location that is secure, accessible, and better equipped to withstand natural disasters.

"The ideal government agency to occupy the building is the American Samoa Visitors Bureau, which is currently leasing office space in Tedi's Building," he said. "Given its location along the main road and adjacent to the Main Wharf, this historic structure would serve as a perfect home for the Visitors Bureau."

He argued that the building's strategic location makes it a natural point of contact for tourists arriving by sea, particularly during cruise ship visits.

"When a cruise ship is in port, passengers typically disembark and walk directly into town. The first place many of them would look for information, directions, and visitor services is the Visitors Bureau," he explained. "Having the bureau located in this historic building would not only provide greater visibility and accessibility for visitors, but it would also breathe new life into the structure and give it a purpose that complements its historical significance."

According to McGuire, converting the building into a tourism information center would create a more welcoming gateway to the Territory while preserving public access to one of American Samoa's most recognizable historic landmarks.

"Instead of fencing it off and limiting its interaction with the public, the building could become a showcase for American Samoa's culture, history, and tourism attractions," he said. "It would be a fitting use for such a prominent and historic property, while the Territorial Registrar's Office could be relocated to a safer and more secure facility better suited for protecting important government records.

"After welcoming visitors to the Territory, the Visitors Bureau staff could share the history of American Samoa as an unincorporated territory of the United States and explain how it was initially administered by the U.S. Navy," he said. "They could then tell the story of the building itself and the important role it played in maintaining communications between American Samoa and other U.S. military and government outposts throughout the Pacific."

He noted that the building's historical significance extends beyond its architectural value and is tied directly to events that helped shape the Territory's history.

Among the stories that could be highlighted, he noted, are the building's vital function as a communications hub during the U.S. Naval Administration, its role in helping authorities respond to the 1918 influenza pandemic, and its participation in the network of radio communications used during the search for famed aviator Amelia Earhart following her disappearance in 1937.

"These are the kinds of stories that visitors would find fascinating," he continued. "They highlight the important role this building and the communications network associated with it played in the history of American Samoa and the wider Pacific. Preserving that history and sharing it with visitors would be a far more meaningful use of the building than simply surrounding it with a fence."

McGuire concluded by urging government officials to postpone any decision on the proposed perimeter fence until a broader public discussion can be held.

He suggested that representatives from the Historic Preservation Office, Port Administration, the American Samoa Visitors Bureau, the Arts Council, preservation organizations, and the public should have an opportunity to weigh in on the long-term future of the historic property before permanent changes are made.

HISTORIC PRESERVATION OFFICE

Samoa News reached out to Tish Peau, Territorial Archaeologist with the Historic Preservation Office (HPO), to explain why she supported the Department of Legal Affairs' request to construct a perimeter fence around the historic building.

According to Peau, her office approved the request because the proposed fence would be a temporary measure until funding becomes available for a future project to raise the building to street level. She explained that when the structure was originally built, it sat at the same grade as the surrounding area. Over time, however, roadwork, development, and natural changes in the landscape caused the surrounding ground level to rise, leaving the building lower than its surroundings and more vulnerable to litter and drainage problems.

Peau said the temporary fence, combined with the proposed roof replacement and gutter installation, would help protect the historic structure from the elements and address the longstanding litter problem while longer-term preservation plans are developed.

McGuire, however, strongly disagreed with the proposal to elevate the building in the future.

"I think the idea of raising this historic building three or four feet off the ground is unrealistic," he said. "In more than 20 years of real estate appraisal experience in American Samoa and California, I have never seen a historic concrete-foundation building lifted that far. The only practical way to do it would be to dismantle the structure and reconstruct it on a higher foundation in its original form, and that would be extremely expensive."

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources (DMWR) marked a significant milestone last Friday with the christening of two new vessels that will strengthen the department's ability to protect American Samoa's marine resources and support fisheries management throughout the Territory.

The ceremony brought Lieutenant Governor Pulumataala Ae Ae Jr., government officials, community partners, DMWR personnel, and invited guests together to celebrate the addition of the Ta'io and Sausauimoana II to the department's operational fleet.

The expansion of the fleet represents an important investment in DMWR's ongoing efforts to safeguard the Territory's vast marine environment, enforce fisheries regulations, and conduct critical field operations in local waters.

Among the highlights of the ceremony was the christening of the Ta'io, a state-of-the-art safe boat manufactured by Safe Boats International, a company based in Seattle. Designed for durability, reliability, and performance in challenging ocean conditions, the vessel is 38 feet long and 12 feet wide and will enhance DMWR's ability to conduct offshore patrols, marine research activities, and emergency response operations.

Present at the christening ceremony was Safe Boats International representative Yehudah Landau, who traveled here for the occasion and will be conducting training for DMWR staff on how to operate the boat.

In an exclusive interview with DMWR Director Nathan Ilaoa, he explained that the new vessel Taʻio was named after the Tahiti Petrel, a rare seabird found in American Samoa that is known for its ability to travel vast distances across the Pacific Ocean, but always finds its way back to its nesting grounds on the mountains of Tutuila. The name reflects the vessel's mission of safeguarding the Territory's marine resources and supporting conservation efforts throughout local waters.

Joining the Ta'io in the fleet is the 32-foot-long enforcement vessel Sausauimoana II, constructed locally through a partnership with Industrial Gases. The boat has been specially customized to support fisheries inspections and monitoring activities, providing DMWR officers with an additional platform for carrying out their regulatory and conservation responsibilities. According to longtime businessman Peter Crispin, the vessel took about three months to build with assistance from Andy Wearing.

Officials noted that the acquisition of the two vessels comes at a critical time as DMWR continues its work to combat illegal fishing activities, monitor fishing fleets, collect scientific data, and ensure the sustainable management of marine resources that are vital to the Territory's economy, food security, and cultural heritage. The Ta'io was purchased with ARPA funds totaling about $900,000, while the Sausauimoana II was purchased with funds from the NOAA Fisheries Office of Law Enforcement.

Speaking during the ceremony, leaders emphasized that the new additions will improve the department's operational reach and increase its ability to respond efficiently to issues affecting local fisheries and marine ecosystems throughout the year.

The vessels are expected to play a key role in supporting inspections, enforcement efforts, marine conservation programs, and resource management initiatives in waters surrounding Tutuila, Aunu'u, Manu'a, Swains Island, and other areas under the Territory's jurisdiction.

The event also highlighted the importance of partnerships between government agencies and private-sector organizations in strengthening American Samoa's marine resource management capabilities.

DMWR Director Ilaoa and his staff were recognized for their efforts in securing and overseeing the acquisition of the vessels, which officials described as a major achievement for the department.

As the ceremony concluded, guests gathered to offer congratulations and blessings for the crews who will operate the vessels and the important work they will carry out in protecting the Territory's ocean resources for future generations.

The christening of the Ta'io and Sausauimoana II signals another step forward in DMWR's mission to conserve American Samoa's marine environment while ensuring that the Territory's fisheries remain healthy, productive, and sustainable for years to come.

Behavioral Health, Drug & Rehabilitation Center Project needs extension to complete

2026-11-10

By

Samoa News staff

reporters@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — House Representative (Faipule) Fagaima Larry Sanitoa’s request to Congresswoman Uifa’atali Aumua Amata for urgent assistance to help the territory obtain deadline extensions for ARPA funds through legislative help did not include specifics about the ARPA-funded projects that are at risk.

The projects are facing a looming December 31, 2026 deadline — to be completed or lose the remaining funding.

Samoa News has learned that one of the projects Fagaima has been asked to help, is the Department of Health (DOH) Behavioral Health, Drug and Rehabilitation Center Project, being built in Tafuna (in the old Tafuna Housing area).

The DOH ARPA Senior Projects manager, on behalf of DOH director Dr. Saipale Fuimaono, prepared a summary report for Fagaima, and provided photos to verify the construction site’s progress or condition to help its request to get an extension.

The report, dated October 13, 2026, an excel document, shows that the overall project is 70% completed. It indicates that delays have been due to shipping, Acts of God, and weather conditions, and lays out that the project’s Phase 6 through 11 are scheduled to be completed in May 2027.

DOH ARPA Senior Projects Manager Falanai M. Ala includes a professional observation or opinion of the construction work. He writes:

The Silva Group has been working very hard at moving this project to its completion. They have worked 7 days a week, and utilizing night shifts when they pour concrete during the Foundation, Slab on Grade, and Brick Laying phases’ many days.

They have been averaging approximately 65 to 75 workers on site daily and sometimes 100 workers  during big concrete pours.  They also have a night crew working on an "as needed basis" during the concrete pours, brick laying, and other construction phases.

The Silva Group is definitely one of the best Contractors the DOH has on its ARPA Construction Projects.  This project is progressing according to schedule, despite all of the difficulty in shipping, work force, and weather delays. This project is approximately 70% overall complete.

The Silva Group has not submitted a single change order as of 10/14/26, considering the fact that this project was design by a third party Architectural Firm name, Jacob Cubitt Architects (JCA) in Australia, through PIOA Consultants.

This is very un-usual and rare for contractors in American Samoa to construct a building this far into the construction process without submitting any change order for the project.

The only change order we are anticipating for this project is the purchase and installation price for the stand-by generator for the BHS Facility. This was not included in the Request for Proposal (RFP) and Scope of work (SOW).

The Silva Group is a company with integrity and high moral character, they treat their employees very well.

He concludes that “the DOH ARPA Team is extremely proud and happy to work with the Silva Group on this project.“

Reported elsewhere in today’s edition, Congresswoman Amata, who is now in Washington D.C. is an update of her efforts to extend the deadline for ARPA funding legislatively, and includes writing a letter to U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent asking for his support.

Gov. Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula made his own request in October 2026 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury for a six-month extension to complete the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) projects.

Amata in her comments on the issue, reminded Samoa News that this is the second time an extension for completion has been requested for ARPA funding, the first request occurred in 2025, which led to the current deadline of December 31, 2026.

Honoring those who have worn our country’s uniform

2026-11-10

By

Samoa News staff

reporters@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — In observance of Veterans Day, Governor Pulaalii Nikolai Pula has declared Wednesday, November 11, 2026 a public holiday in American Samoa. All ASG offices will be closed, with normal government operation resuming on Thursday, November 12, 2026,  Department directors and agency heads are reminded to ensure essential government services remain operational as necessary.

“On behalf of Lieutenant Governor Pulumataala and the Administration, we express our sincere gratitude to all veterans and their families, particularly our sons and daughters, for their service and sacrifice. We honor the courage and dedication of those who served in United States Armed Forces to defend our nation and uphold our freedoms. Happy Veterans Day! God bless our veterans, and God bless American Samoa,” Governor Pulaali i Nikolao Pula said in general memorandum issued over the weekend.

Congresswoman Uifa’atali Aumua Amata who serves as Vice Chairman of the House Veterans’ Affairs Committee is honoring U.S. Veterans and especially thanking American Samoa’s Veterans this Veterans Day.

“Thank you to our Veterans, and have a blessed Veterans Day. You mean so much to our islands, and we appreciate your leadership and wisdom,” said Congresswoman Amata. “I am humbled to serve our Veterans on the Committee, where we constantly hear from our Veterans and work for improved performance from the VA, based on that input from Veterans and Service Organizations.

“Thank you to each one for your service and patriotism,” continued Amata. “ As a nation, we have made an enduring national commitment to all our veterans for their care and wellbeing, at every age. This includes their healthcare, assisting transitions out of the Armed Forces, furthering their second careers or higher education, to hospice, burial services and dignified funeral honors, as well as survivor benefits and comfort. Our Veterans should know their families are secure.

“Like so many of us in American Samoa, my father and brothers served, and we love and honor our Veterans and our military families. May God protect our Service Members, and bless and uphold our Veterans.”

On Monday, the House was scheduled to vote on the bipartisan Veterans’ Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2026. The bill increases the rates of compensation for veterans with service-connected disabilities, and the rates of dependency and indemnity compensation for the survivors of certain disabled veterans.

The US Postal Service Office and the Territorial Bank of American Samoa will be closed in observance of Veterans Day, tomorrow.

In honor of Veterans Day, Samoa News offices will also be closed and there will be no Wednesday issue. Samoa News will finish out the week with issues on Thursday and Friday.

BACKGROUND

Originally established as Armistice Day in 1919 by President Woodrow Wilson to mark the first anniversary of the end of World War I (hostilities formally ceased on the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month in 1918).

Renamed Veterans Day in 1954 under President Dwight D. Eisenhower to honor all American veterans who served in ll wars and conflicts, distinguishing it from Memorial Day, which specifically remembers those who died while in service.

Veterans Day honors all living and deceased men and women who have served in the United States Armed Forces.

It is observed on November 11th, regardless of what day of the week on which it falls. When it was originally signed into law in 1968, with three other national holidays— Washington’s Birthday (Presidents Day), Memorial Day, and Columbus Day (Discovers Day) — all four were established to be three-day weekends for Federal employees to celebrate on a Monday.

According to the Veterans Affairs website, “It was thought that these extended weekends would encourage travel, recreational and cultural activities and stimulate greater industrial and commercial production.”

However, it was restored to be observed on November 11 (no matter which day it fell on) in 1975 by President Gerald R. Ford, returning the annual observance of Veterans Day to its original date of November 11, beginning in 1978. It is now observed on the day the date falls.

This action, according to Veteran Affairs, supported the desires of the overwhelming majority of state legislatures, all major veterans service organizations and the American people to preserve the historical significance of the date.

It also helps focus attention on the important purpose of Veterans Day: A celebration to honor America’s veterans for their patriotism, love of country, and willingness to serve and sacrifice for the common good.

National STEM Day encourages learning in science, technology, engineering and mathematics

2026-11-09

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — National STEM Day was celebrated yesterday, November 8 to encourage kids to explore their interests in the core subjects — science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM). The observance traces back to 2015 when a toy company aimed to inspire kids to pursue STEM fields through play.

Congresswoman Congresswoman Uifa'atali Aumua Amata’s office released the following statement on the yearly event:

As the global economy continues to grow and technology brings our world closer together, STEM education is more important than ever. Thank you to our educators in American Samoa helping to ensure our students have the knowledge and skills necessary to compete in an increasingly technology-driven world. Math and science education are driving forces for the future of business, innovation, and our economy.

Pacific Islanders have an excellent opportunity to advance in STEM fields. These careers are not limited to major cities, offering our students the opportunity to contribute to the global workforce while remaining connected to their island communities. We must ensure that our children here are not being left behind by increasing opportunities to explore their abilities in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics in our local schools.

I am committed with you to ensuring that the youth of American Samoa are afforded the same opportunities and resources as their counterparts in the states, at every level from Head Start and elementary schools to high school and college. I look forward to continuing to work with our territory’s education leaders and my colleagues in Congress to support STEM education and prepare the next generation for the opportunities ahead.

This year, Congress designated $3 million of the growing American Samoa operations fund at my request to support needs at ASCC, and our bill (the Territorial Student Access to Higher Education Act, H.R. 6472) to provide students from the territories with in-state rates for university tuition is closer than ever. We’ve worked on this education policy for years, secured House-wide bipartisan support, and I will continue working for final passage.

The American Community Survey estimates that more than 41.6 million Americans ages 25 and older held a bachelor’s degree or higher in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics or a related field in 2025, representing roughly 47 percent of all people with a bachelor’s degree or higher.

Pacific Horizons School receives donation from the Lealaifuaneva Peter E. Reid Charitable Foundation

2026-11-06

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Pacific Horizons School (PHS) is pleased to announce receiving a generous $20,000 donation from the Lealaifuaneva Peter E. Reid Charitable Foundation in support of the PHS 2nd Annual Giving Campaign. This contribution represents a significant investment in the school’s mission to provide high-quality educational opportunities for students in American Samoa.

The PHS Annual Giving Campaign was launched in 2025 to help secure the school’s long-term future amid changes to federal Consolidated Grant funding. This grant offset approximately 15% of the school’s operating costs. With restrictions now in place, PHS faces a deficit that poses challenges to maintaining its programs.

The Giving Campaign invites community partners to serve as “Anchor Donors,” aligning with the school’s nautical theme, by helping PHS reach its $70,000 goal. This support will directly strengthen the school’s general fund and ensure continued access to high-quality, well-rounded education for future generations.

Pacific Horizons School extends its warmest thanks to the Lealaifuaneva Peter E. Reid Charitable Foundation for its partnership and philanthropy. Their support helps make it possible for PHS to continue building a strong, innovative, and student-centered future.

For more information about the PHS Annual Giving Campaign or ways to support, please contact Veronica Soto, School Director at veronicasoto@pacific-horizons-school.com (684) 699-5787.
